lifecycleCoverage.note: The delivery lifecycle exists end to end: lead capture, requirements, design and prototype with client review, module tracking, QA with a gate, milestone billing, handover holding no secrets, a client portal, and an end-of-project summary. What remains is the layer after delivery - maintenance, client success, upsell - and the gates that need business rules.

gaps.title: Nothing marks an invoice overdue
gaps.evidence: finance.mark_overdue_invoices runs on the cron tick and performs the transition INVOICE_TRANSITIONS has admitted since the first day: issued and partially_paid become overdue once due_at has passed. Not a new rule - an existing one executed for the first time. It takes each row for update skip locked, restates the status on the write so a payment landing in the same instant wins, and audits only what it actually changed. It chases nobody: a payment reminder is client-facing and waits on the outbound policy rather than arriving behind a status change. Five statuses are deliberately untouched - draft, pending_approval, paid, void, and anything with no due date.

gaps.title: Refunds unimplemented
gaps.evidence: finance.refunds records money going back as its own row, because finance/schema.ts has said since the first day that paid is terminal and money returned is a refund rather than a status flip. Three rules, none invented here: a refund needs an approved approval behind it (directive 28 RED, 29 the Admin's; the engine already carried 'refund' as a subject type and its money floor already refused any policy naming below owner); it cannot exceed what came in, computed under the invoice lock and refused rather than clamped, counting requests still waiting so two owners cannot approve the same balance; and the invoice is untouched. Recording is idempotent on the provider reference, re-checks the ceiling because an approval from yesterday must still fit today, and both the asking and the leaving are audited. The invoice screen now drives it: refunds are listed with their state, an owner may ask for one against the available balance, and recording that the money left is a separate control - one control doing both would be a refund with no approval behind it. Neither the form nor the action inspects the approval; the database refuses an unapproved recording and a copy of that rule in TypeScript could drift.

gaps.evidence: Built under ADM-09, taken by delegation: the inbound webhook already speaks WhatsApp Cloud API, so outbound over the same Graph API adds no vendor. crm.send_outbound_message records the message BEFORE the provider is called - a message sent and not recorded is invisible, a message recorded and not sent is visibly wrong - allocating seq under the conversation's lock and deduplicating on the caller's idempotency key. The number and the sending account are read from the database, so one organization cannot send as another. What the provider says is written back by crm.mark_outbound_delivery, which audits from inside its own transaction and refuses to re-settle a message. Inert without WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN, and it says so rather than appearing to work.

gaps.title: Development module tracking
gaps.evidence: projects.modules gives a project its actual pieces - customer app, backend, vendor panel - with directive 16's own status vocabulary, deliberately coarser than a task's, and the task state machine untouched because the directive warns against inventing a second one. Tasks and deliverables carry a nullable module_id; a trigger refuses one naming a module from another project, which no foreign key prevents and which would otherwise put a task in another project's progress. projects.module_progress answers how each piece is going, counting its tasks and the open defects against builds of it.

gaps.title: Client development review
gaps.evidence: A build is a deliverable of kind 'build', versioned and reviewed through the approval engine with its changelog and known issues. What was missing is directive 17's test credentials: deliverables.test_access_method records HOW a client gets in and refuses the three shapes somebody actually pastes - password:, pin:, api_key: - which is an accident stopper rather than a secret detector, and says so. Immutable once recorded, like everything else on a version.

gaps.title: Project official start has no conditions
Milestone unlock is advisory
No qa schema
gaps.evidence: qa.defects carries what directive 19 asks of every bug: severity, reproduction (required - a bug nobody can reproduce is a rumour), expected, actual, environment, evidence, assignee, status, resolution and verification. ARCHITECTURE.md 4.8's vocabulary is kept as written. The gate it states is enforced inside projects.submit_deliverable, under the same lock that writes the status. Scoped to the version and to project-wide defects rather than to the project: a blocker on v1 must not stop v2, because v2 is the fix, and the project-wide reading would make the fix unshowable and reward closing bugs dishonestly.

gaps.title: Production-ready gate
gaps.evidence: Written up for a decision: docs/decisions/g-031-production-ready.md. Until this week the question was unanswerable - no defect table, no versioned deliverables, no handover. Every fact a gate would need is now measurable and named in the document, along with the four conditions directive 20 lists that AgencyOS has never held: a client build succeeding, its deployment, its security checks and its documentation are facts about the client's project that this system does not observe, and a gate claiming to check them would be lying. Four questions (hard versus advisory, who may override and is it recorded, per project or per organization, and whether readiness gates anything at all) and three shapes: a readout, a hard gate on measurable conditions only, or that plus an owner-approved recorded override. The last is recommended - but only if readiness gates something, since otherwise it is ceremony.

gaps.title: Handover
gaps.evidence: projects.handovers and projects.handover_items record what was delivered, when, and whether the client said they had it. Directive 22's credentials rule shaped the schema: a credential item is incapable of holding a credential - reference must be null and transfer_method must say how it actually reached the client, refused in DDL rather than by a service that could forget. Delivery refuses an empty package and refuses while an open blocker or major defect stands (ARCHITECTURE.md 4.8, directive 20). The outstanding balance is reported and NOT gated on, because which payment is final is the project's own plan and inventing that rule would put a made-up gate in front of real revenue. Acceptance is the client's, through the approval engine, which gains 'handover' as a subject type.

gaps.title: Project completion summary
gaps.evidence: projects.completion_summary assembles directive 23's end-of-project figures from five tables that already held every fact: budget, invoiced, paid and outstanding as four separate numbers because they differ often enough that collapsing any two hides the interesting case; duration, null while the project runs because a duration measured to now() reads as a fact and is a moving number; milestones met, versions, revisions counted as versions beyond the first PER KIND, the final approved version, defects open and total, and the handover status. It is a read: it marks nothing complete and gates on nothing, because what these numbers imply about closing a project is ADM-13/ADM-14 and ADM-19.

gaps.title: Maintenance and support
Approved offer catalog
Upsell engine
Client lifetime model
No approval engine
gaps.evidence: Built as ARCHITECTURE.md 4.6 designs it, under ADM-08. approvals.approval_requests serves all eight subject types and both audiences; approvals.approval_policies holds who must decide, as owner-editable data with a money floor in DDL. The required role is snapshotted onto each request so a policy edited mid-flight cannot change the rule a pending request was raised under. Raising is idempotent through a partial unique index; deciding takes a row lock and a compare-and-swap; the tables accept no direct writes at all, so a role can never settle through PostgREST what the function would have refused. Every request and decision is audited from inside its own transaction.

gaps.title: Automation trust levels not enforced
gaps.evidence: ai.agents.autonomy_level was selected by the job runner and then ignored, which is worse than not reading it: the code looked as though autonomy were configurable while the behaviour was L1 whatever the row said, so turning an agent down was a deploy. Enforced twice now. src/lib/ai/autonomy.ts decides - L1 acts, L0 is read-only, L2 is refused because accepting its own proposal needs a stated policy (G-101) and silently behaving as L1 would tell an operator something untrue about their deployment, and an unrecognised level is refused rather than defaulted. The runner checks it before reaching the model, for the message and the settled job; ai.agent_runs_autonomy_guard refuses the same thing independently, so a script or a future worker cannot skip it. Proved live: the identical call succeeds at L1 and is refused one UPDATE later.

gaps.title: invoice.created is still published after its transaction
gaps.testCoverage: tests/outbox-transactional.test.ts section E (4) and tests/audit-in-the-transaction.test.ts section F, both flipped from pinning the gap to asserting it closed; scripts/verify-milestone-invoicing.mjs section 7h (12 live checks) against real Postgres.
gaps.evidence: Closed. finance.create_milestone_invoice writes the invoice, its lines, its audit row and its invoice.created event in one statement. It used to be four transactions with a hand-rolled compensating DELETE between the first two - a rollback that runs only if the process lives long enough to run it. The P3 rating rested on nothing subscribing to invoice.created, which was a fact about the subscription catalog rather than about the invoice; the audit row was never covered by that argument at all, because audit.audit_log is append-only and a row never written can never be repaired. Deliberately left in TypeScript: which lines an invoice has and what its number is, both pure and tested, because re-deriving either in plpgsql is how regenerating replace_payment_plan silently reverted D16. Two refusals moved from application pre-checks to index violations, so a request arriving between a check and its insert can no longer slip through the gap - the shape D1, D2 and D4 all were. The constraint name is read from the diagnostics rather than matched out of SQLERRM, which is prose and therefore translated. The live section proves the half that matters: a line the database refuses leaves no invoice, no history, no event, and a milestone still billable.

gaps.title: messages already filed under the wrong tenant are not repaired
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/verify-tenancy-overlap.mjs (2 checks), run against local, CI and production
gaps.evidence: Answered rather than repaired, and the answer changes the decision. The ingest keys a thread on the SENDER's number - 'wa:' || phone - and never records the number a message arrived on, so which organization SHOULD have received an existing row is not recoverable from the row, the conversation or the message. Any tool claiming to identify mis-filed rows in general would be guessing. Two things can be established and both are: whether two organizations claim one number today, and the only detectable fingerprint - one phone number appearing under more than one organization. Run against production: one organization, no WhatsApp number configured, three contacts, zero overlap. There is nothing to move or delete, so the decision this gap was waiting on has no rows to apply to. That the blindness would recur is G-102.

gaps.title: nothing expires an unanswered approval request
gaps.testCoverage: tests/approval-engine.test.ts F, scripts/verify-approvals.mjs section 11 (8 live checks)
gaps.evidence: approvals.expire_overdue settles every pending request past its own deadline as expired and raises a fresh one against the owner, linked by escalated_from, from the cron tick. The original is left exactly as it was - it is the evidence that somebody did not answer - and the escalation gets the same window measured from now, so the owner is not given less time than the person who missed it. It escalates once, because there is nobody above the owner. It cannot approve: there is no path from here to approved, and decide_approval refuses a caller with no identity, which a cron tick is. Two overlapping ticks cannot both expire one request - the claim is for update skip locked.

gaps.evidence: The specific case was fixed when the approvals schema shipped unreachable - the migration appends itself to pgrst.db_schemas. gaps.testCoverage: tests/approval-centre.test.ts - twelve behavioural tests over an action module
gaps.evidence: next/cache does not resolve outside a Next build, so importing any 'use server' module from the test runner failed with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Action tests therefore asserted on source text - structural assertions standing in for behaviour, which directive 38 permits only as a supplement. tests/_alias.mjs now maps next/cache to an inert stub, so an action is an ordinary module of async functions again and its outcome mapping can be driven for real. gaps.title: a dead job cannot be requeued from anywhere
gaps.testCoverage: tests/job-requeue.test.ts (23), scripts/verify-operational-backlog.mjs section 5 (12 live checks) - including the one a structural test cannot make, that a running job is refused and left with its claim intact.
gaps.evidence: Closed. core.requeue_job sends one dead job back to the queue. The idempotency story the gap asked for turned out to already exist, and the argument is the feature: a dead job is one the runner already attempted max_attempts times, so requeuing is a sixth attempt of something the queue makes five of unattended - a handler that cannot survive a replay is already broken, and was before this existed. Both handlers were written for it in the database rather than by the queue being careful: milestone.unlock carries status = 'pending' in the UPDATE predicate and answers already_unlocked, requirement_versions_transcript_state_key makes a second extraction of an unchanged transcript conflict. What needed protecting was the queue's own bookkeeping - only a dead job may be reset, decided under a row lock, because resetting a running job is the one way to get the same work claimed twice, and the row is reused rather than re-inserted so jobs_dedupe_key_key still holds. last_error is kept: the operator read it in order to decide, and clearing it would erase the reason at the moment somebody acted on it. Audited inside the transaction per G-079. New capability job.requeue for owner and ops_admin rather than reusing audit.read, whose role set is identical but which is a read.

gaps.title: an approved deliverable gates nothing
gaps.evidence: Written up for a decision: docs/decisions/g-100-approvals-and-payments.md. Two mechanisms exist and do not touch - money flows on payment (invoice paid unlocks the next milestone) and approval flows on delivery (a version is approved by the client through the engine) - so directive 18's middle arrow, UI_APPROVED to MILESTONE_PAYMENT_DUE, does not exist. A milestone also has no column linking it to a deliverable, so every option but the status quo needs one. Three questions (does approval release a payment or merely permit it; does an unpaid invoice block handover; per project or template) and four shapes. B is recommended - approval permits issuing, refusing only the act that reaches the client, which is the shape the QA gate already uses. C is explicitly not recommended: every other money path here requires a human, and making the first exception a client's click deserves to be chosen rather than inherited.

gaps.title: what L2 autonomy means has never been stated
gaps.testCoverage: tests/agent-autonomy.test.ts B - an L2 agent must be refused while this is open
gaps.evidence: ai.agents.autonomy_level admits L2 and the schema calls it 'autonomous within limits'. For the one agent that exists, autonomous would mean accepting its own requirement proposal with no human, which directive 29 forbids without a stated policy. L2 is therefore refused rather than treated as L1 - an operator who sets it should be told they did not get autonomy. What L2 may do, and within which limits, is the Admin's to say.

gaps.title: the number a message arrived on is never recorded
gaps.testCoverage: tests/crm-ingest.test.ts H (4), scripts/verify-whatsapp-ingest.mjs E, scripts/verify-tenancy-overlap.mjs section 3
gaps.evidence: crm.conversations.inbound_number_id records which of the agency's numbers a thread arrived on - the value the ingest already resolved tenancy from and then discarded, which is what made G-090 unanswerable. Nullable and not backfilled: a conversation predating the column came in on a number nobody recorded, and inventing one would repeat the guess D22 was. How it was changed matters as much as what changed - the function is frozen since D22, was redefined once since by the terminal-lead migration, and regenerating it from the file that introduced it is exactly how G-079's verification caught a silent revert of D16. The body is pg_get_functiondef of the live function with one edit, and a diff before and after shows only the two intended lines. The tenancy report now makes the check G-090 could not: a conversation filed under an organization that does not claim its number.

gaps.title: nine verification scripts crashed instead of explaining an incomplete environment
gaps.testCoverage: Proved red: a truncated .env.verify.local now prints the missing variable instead of "fail is not a function"
gaps.evidence: resolveTarget takes the caller's own exit function as its first argument, and every script added this session passed none - so on an incomplete environment they raised TypeError: fail is not a function instead of the sentence naming what was missing. They also inherited the default needs, which demands CRON_SECRET, though none of them calls the job runner. Found by accident while pointing a script at production with a truncated env file: the error path nobody had executed.

gaps.title: the change log stopped being kept, and two merge gates were carried open after merging
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/check-record.mjs sections 7 and 8, run by `npm run check` and by CI on every pull request. Proved red first against the unreconciled record: twenty-three unlogged merges and two gates, three failures, exit 1.
gaps.evidence: G-094 closed the numbers and left the events. Twenty-three pull requests merged with no change-log row - every one of 2026-08-13's work - and the log's final entry still described itself as '(this change)' for a change that had landed the day before. In the same document, section 4.8 said ADM-46 through ADM-49 were all granted while section 5 and this file carried ADM-47 and ADM-48 as open, a day after the pull requests they gated merged. Both were in fact granted under the blanket delegation of 2026-08-13, which is what the merges rested on; the failure is that nobody wrote it down, and the checker could not see either drift because it re-derives numbers and reads nothing about what happened. Two checks now: every pull request number appearing in a commit subject must appear in the change log, singly or in a recorded range, and a merge gate may not stay open once every gap it blocks is classed A. The first needs full git history, so CI's check job no longer shallow-clones - and refuses to run in a shallow clone rather than reporting 'covers all 0 merges', which is what it printed when it was measured against a depth-1 clone of its own branch. A check whose job is to notice an absence must not be the one that passes vacuously.

gaps.title: the change-log check demanded the newest merge's row immediately, so main went red the moment it shipped
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/check-record.mjs section 7. Measured both ways: green on main with #65 outstanding, and red for #65 once a later merge is stacked on top, so the exemption cannot be held open.
gaps.evidence: G-104's section 7 required a change-log row for every merge including the newest. The convention it exists to enforce is that a pull request cannot record its own merge approval - the change after it writes the row - so there is always exactly one merge outstanding, and the check did not say so. The first thing it did after merging was turn main red for PR #65, itself. A red main between every merge and the next change is how a team learns to merge past a red check, which is the same failure as an alert nobody reads. Only the newest merge is exempt now, and the pass line names it rather than staying quiet: 'with #65 outstanding for the next change to record'. One more merge and the previous number is no longer newest, so at most one may be outstanding - the convention written as an invariant. The twenty-three unlogged merges that raised G-104 would still fail here, twenty-two times.

gaps.title: the non-transactional publish path has no callers and is still exported
gaps.testCoverage: tests/outbox-transactional.test.ts section F (3). Mutation-tested three ways: the file returning, a second publisher appended late in a file whose first outbox call is a legitimate select, and a publisher in a brand new file. The second of those failed to be caught on the first draft and is why the check scans every occurrence rather than the first.
gaps.evidence: Closed by deletion. src/lib/events/index.ts held only emitEvent and its type and had no caller in src or app once G-078 landed. Deleting it is only half the fix - without a check, the second version gets written the next time somebody needs an event and finds no helper - so section F states the property rather than guarding a filename: no file under src or app inserts into core.outbox_events, under any name, and the only file touching the table at all is lib/events/dispatch.ts, which reads it and stamps published_at. Nine test files mocked the module; their mocks are gone with it. Four assertions that watched the mocked emitEvent to prove the service publishes nothing would have become unfailable, so they now assert the service never reached for the outbox table at all - which the stub clients already recorded. payment-ledger's stub did not record tables and now does.

gaps.title: a gap could require an Admin decision that nobody could find
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/check-record.mjs section 8. Proved red first against the unreconciled record: G-091 and G-095, exit 1. Mutation-tested with a planted row that says Yes and names nothing.
gaps.evidence: Section 4's gap table has a column for whether the Admin must decide something. Two rows said Yes and named nothing, so neither decision appeared in section 5, in the decision counts, or in any list of what the Admin owes - and a reader grouping the open gaps by their blocking decision files them under 'none', which reads as unblocked. Not hypothetical: G-091 was picked up as available work during this session on exactly that reading, and only reading the row itself showed it needed an answer first. ADM-57 and ADM-58 raised for the two. The check counts a cited pull request as findable, not only an ADM id, because twenty-four rows cite a merge approval from before the one-decision-per-PR convention existed and inventing ADM numbers for them now would be writing history rather than recording it. A cited PR is something a reader can go and look at; a bare Yes is not.

adminDecisions.title: Verifying a WhatsApp number: ask Meta, or gate the setting behind a review?
adminDecisions.why: An owner can set their organization's whatsapp_phone_number_id to a number they do not own. Since D22's unique index the effect is no longer a silent capture - it is a denial of configuration, because the rightful agency's write is then refused with a bare 409. Two shapes: verify ownership against the Graph API at configuration time, which needs a token with permission to ask and must decide what to do when Meta is unreachable; or leave the field free and gate it behind an operator review, which needs somebody to do the reviewing. Neither is obviously right, and the current behaviour - first writer wins, permanently - is the one nobody chose. This row said an Admin decision was required and named none, which is G-107.

adminDecisions.title: May the unsupported snapshot be made to refuse to run?

The marking is prose and prose does not stop a paste: the file still opens a transaction and still builds a schema missing D16, D17-D22, G-079, G-082, G-083 and G-084. One line - a raise exception before the begin - makes it refuse rather than warn, at the cost of the file no longer being runnable even deliberately. That trade was not part of what ADM-40 was offered, which is why it was recorded rather than taken.
